78:         if match_support != 'available' or match_scaling != 'norm':
79:             raise ValueError('This study freezes the incumbent fifth support and scale')
80:         if coarse_extension not in ('cubic', 'scrambled', 'duplicate', 'bridge'):
81:             raise ValueError('Unknown coarse ordinal replacement')
82:         self.coarse_extension = coarse_extension
83:         if primary_partition not in ('aligned', 'rotated', 'uniform'):
84:             raise ValueError('Unknown primary partition readout')
85:         if primary_partition != 'uniform':
86:             raise ValueError('This study fixes the primary uniform readout')
87:         self.primary_partition = primary_partition
88:         if normalization_support not in ('aligned_rotated', 'rotated_duplicate'):
89:             raise ValueError('Unknown Dice support population')
90:         if support_gradient not in ('attached', 'blocked'):
91:             raise ValueError('Unknown support preactivation gradient')
92:         self.normalization_support = normalization_support
93:         self.support_gradient = support_gradient
94:         self.embedding_layer = FeatureEmbeddingDict(feature_map, embedding_dim)
95:         self.item_fields = [name for name, spec in feature_map.features.items()
96:                             if spec.get('source') == 'item' and spec['type'] != 'meta']
97:         self.user_fields = [name for name, spec in feature_map.features.items()
98:                             if spec.get('source') not in ('item', 'action')
99:                             and spec['type'] != 'meta']
100:         self.action_field = next((name for name, spec in feature_map.features.items()
101:                                   if spec.get('source') == 'action'), None)
102:         if self.action_field is None:
103:             raise ValueError('Historical action field is required')
104:         self.auxiliary_indices = [list(feature_map.labels).index(label)
105:                                   for label in ('cart', 'fav', 'buy')]
106:         self.key_width = len(self.item_fields) * embedding_dim
107:         self.value_width = self.key_width + embedding_dim
108:         # Only supplied encoded fields are compared; no external lookups.
109:         # Zero and declared special IDs never constitute positive evidence.
110:         self.match_fields = ('item_id', 'cate_id', 'brand')
111:         self.match_excluded_ids = {}
112:         for name in self.match_fields:
113:             if name not in self.item_fields:
114:                 raise ValueError('Required target-match field is absent: ' + name)
115:             spec = feature_map.features[name]
116:             excluded = {0}
117:             for special in ('padding_idx', 'oov_idx'):
118:                 if spec.get(special) is not None:
119:                     excluded.add(int(spec[special]))
120:             self.match_excluded_ids[name] = tuple(sorted(excluded))
121: 
122:         # Inherit the action-aware scorer and towers from the previous factorial.
123:         # All cells instantiate exactly the same modules in exactly this order.
124:         layers = []
125:         width = 4 * self.key_width + embedding_dim
126:         for hidden in attention_hidden_units:
127:             layers.extend([nn.Linear(width, hidden), Dice(hidden)])
128:             width = hidden
129:         layers.append(nn.Linear(width, 1))
130:         self.local_activation = nn.Sequential(*layers)
131:         input_width = len(self.user_fields) * embedding_dim + self.key_width + self.value_width
132:         self.towers = nn.ModuleList()
133:         for _ in feature_map.labels:
134:             tower = []
135:             width = input_width
136:             for hidden in tower_hidden_units:
137:                 tower.extend([nn.Linear(width, hidden), Dice(hidden)])
138:                 width = hidden
139:             tower.append(nn.Linear(width, 1))
140:             self.towers.append(nn.Sequential(*tower))
141:         self.reset_parameters()
142:         # No change to inherited modules, their initialization or host RNG.
143:         # Zero final layers give source-equivalent predictions initially.
144:         with torch.random.fork_rng(devices=[]):
145:             self.residual_bank = nn.ModuleList([
146:                 nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(input_width + len(self.match_fields) + 5 * self.value_width,
147:                                         residual_hidden), nn.ReLU(),
148:                               nn.Linear(residual_hidden, self.value_width))
149:                 for _ in feature_map.labels
150:             ])
151:             for adapter in self.residual_bank:
152:                 nn.init.zeros_(adapter[-1].weight)
153:                 nn.init.zeros_(adapter[-1].bias)
154:         self.model_to_device()

156:     def _represent(self, inputs):
157:         # Do not allow the framework fallback that treats every event as
158:         # positive for every task when historical masks are missing.
159:         if len(inputs) != 4:
160:             raise ValueError('Released historical task masks are required')
161:         supplied = inputs[3]
162:         if isinstance(supplied, (list, tuple)):
163:             if len(supplied) != self.num_tasks:
164:                 raise ValueError('Wrong number of historical task masks')
165:         elif torch.is_tensor(supplied):
166:             if supplied.ndim != 3 or supplied.shape[0] != self.num_tasks:
167:                 raise ValueError('Expected historical masks with shape [4,B,100]')
168:         else:
169:             raise ValueError('Released historical task masks are required')
170:         user, item, mask, task_masks = self.get_inputs(inputs, return_multi_masks=True)
171:         if mask.ndim != 2 or mask.shape[1] != 100:
172:             raise ValueError('Frozen protocol requires 100 history positions')
173:         auxiliary = torch.zeros_like(mask, dtype=torch.bool)
174:         for index in self.auxiliary_indices:
175:             if task_masks[index].shape != mask.shape:
176:                 raise ValueError('Historical task mask shape mismatch')
177:             auxiliary = auxiliary | (task_masks[index] > 0)
178:         auxiliary = auxiliary & mask.bool()
179:         user_emb = self.embedding_layer(user)
180:         item_emb = self.embedding_layer(item)
181:         target = torch.cat([item_emb[name][:, -1] for name in self.item_fields], dim=-1)
182:         keys = torch.cat([item_emb[name][:, :-1] for name in self.item_fields], dim=-1)
183:         # Current action is unknown and never enters either summary or scorer.
184:         values = torch.cat([keys, item_emb[self.action_field][:, :-1]], dim=-1)
185:         context = torch.cat([user_emb[name] for name in self.user_fields], dim=-1)
186:         detail, position_detail, block_detail, curvature_detail, joint_detail, match_counts, match_union = self._target_match_summary(
187:             item, values, mask)
188:         return context, target, values, mask, auxiliary, detail, position_detail, block_detail, curvature_detail, joint_detail, match_counts, match_union

190:     def _target_match_summary(self, item, values, mask):
191:         """Five masked value summaries; only the fifth direction/gate varies.
192: 
193:         Quadratic/scrambled coefficients are orthogonal to valid constants
194:         and coarse linear ranks under event-count weighting. A common gate
195:         excludes fewer than three occupied blocks and degenerate residuals.
196:         All fourth coefficients match the inherited coarse coefficient norm.
197:         Duplicate coefficients copy that coarse vector and add no new moment.
198:         FP32 coefficient construction precedes the inherited bf16 contraction.
199:         """
200:         matches = []
201:         for name in self.match_fields:
202:             ids = item[name]
203:             if ids.ndim != 2 or ids.shape[1] != 101 or ids.shape[0] != mask.shape[0]:
204:                 raise ValueError('Expected target-match IDs with shape [B,101]')
205:             history_ids, target_id = ids[:, :-1], ids[:, -1:]
206:             valid = mask.bool() & (history_ids > 0) & (target_id > 0)
207:             for special in self.match_excluded_ids[name]:
208:                 valid = valid & (history_ids != special) & (target_id != special)
209:             matches.append(valid & (history_ids == target_id))
210:         match_matrix = torch.stack(matches, dim=-1).to(torch.float32)
211:         match_counts = torch.log1p(match_matrix.sum(dim=1))
212:         batch, length, width = values.shape
213:         if length != 100:
214:             raise ValueError('Frozen target-match compression requires 100 history positions')
215:         valid = mask.bool().reshape(batch, 10, 10).to(torch.float32)
216:         counts = valid.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
217:         affinity = match_matrix.mean(dim=-1).reshape(batch, 10, 10)
218:         centered = affinity - valid * (affinity.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
219:                                       / counts.clamp_min(1))
220:         # Retain the incumbent within-block ordinal moment without changes.
221:         position = torch.arange(10, device=values.device, dtype=torch.float32).view(1, 1, 10) / 9.0
222:         position_sum = (position * valid).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
223:         centered_position = valid * (position - position_sum / counts.clamp_min(1))
224:         # Coarse ordinals add only information missing under whole-block
225:         # permutations. Center using event counts, including partial blocks.
226:         total = counts.sum(dim=1).clamp_min(1)
227:         block_rank = torch.arange(10, device=values.device, dtype=torch.float32).view(1, 10, 1) / 9.0
228:         block_mean = (block_rank * valid).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True) / total.unsqueeze(-1)
229:         centered_block = valid * (block_rank - block_mean)
230:         local_norm2 = centered_position.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
231:         block_norm2 = centered_block.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
232:         centered_block = (centered_block * (local_norm2 / block_norm2.clamp_min(1e-12)).sqrt()
233:                           * (block_norm2 > 1e-12).to(valid.dtype))
234:         # Retain the inherited coarse coefficient construction, including its
235:         # unused local duplicate, identically in all fourth-channel cells.
236:         duplicated_position = centered_position * (block_norm2 > 1e-12).to(valid.dtype)
237:         block_coefficients = (centered_block if self.block_detail == 'ordinal'
238:                               else duplicated_position)
239:         # Work with the unscaled centered block rank. Its constant and
240:         # linear span is independent of the incumbent norm matching above.
241:         linear = valid * (block_rank - block_mean)
242:         linear_norm2 = linear.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
243:         quadratic_raw = (block_rank - block_mean).square()
244:         # One fixed, predeclared permutation; no sample identities or RNG.
245:         scrambled_rank = torch.tensor(
246:             [0, 7, 2, 9, 4, 1, 8, 3, 6, 5],
247:             device=values.device, dtype=torch.float32).view(1, 10, 1) / 9.0
248:         scrambled_raw = scrambled_rank.square()
249:         quadratic, quadratic_norm2 = self._orthogonal_block_residual(
250:             quadratic_raw, linear, linear_norm2, valid, total)
251:         scrambled, scrambled_norm2 = self._orthogonal_block_residual(
252:             scrambled_raw, linear, linear_norm2, valid, total)
253:         occupied = (counts > 0).sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)
254:         support = ((occupied >= 3) & (quadratic_norm2 > 1e-10)
255:                    & (scrambled_norm2 > 1e-10)).to(valid.dtype)
256:         target_norm2 = centered_block.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
257:         quadratic = (quadratic * (target_norm2 / quadratic_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10)).sqrt()
258:                      * support)
259:         scrambled = (scrambled * (target_norm2 / scrambled_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10)).sqrt()
260:                      * support)
261:         duplicate = centered_block * support
262:         if self.curvature_detail == 'quadratic':
263:             fourth = quadratic
264:         elif self.curvature_detail == 'scrambled':
265:             fourth = scrambled
266:         else:
267:             fourth = duplicate
268:         incumbent_fifth = self._joint_coefficients(
269:             centered, centered_position, fourth, valid, counts,
270:             block_rank, scrambled_rank)
271:         fifth = self._coarse_extension_coefficients(
272:             incumbent_fifth, centered_position, fourth, linear,
273:             block_rank, scrambled_rank, valid, counts, total)
274:         coefficients = torch.stack(
275:             (centered, centered_position, block_coefficients, fourth, fifth), dim=-2)
276:         summaries = torch.bmm(
277:             coefficients.to(values.dtype).reshape(batch * 10, 5, 10),
278:             values.reshape(batch * 10, 10, width))
279:         summaries = summaries.reshape(batch, 10, 5, width).sum(dim=1)
280:         summaries = summaries / total.sqrt().unsqueeze(-1).to(summaries.dtype)
281:         return (summaries[:, 0, :], summaries[:, 1, :], summaries[:, 2, :],
282:                 summaries[:, 3, :], summaries[:, 4, :], match_counts,
283:                 match_matrix.bool().any(dim=-1))
284: 
285:     def _coarse_extension_coefficients(self, incumbent, position, quadratic,
286:                                        linear, rank, scrambled_rank,
287:                                        valid, counts, total):
288:         """Replace the redundant fifth direction at fixed learned capacity.
289: 
290:         Event-weighted projection uses the actual validity mask, including
291:         partial/noncontiguous blocks. Every candidate coefficient is block
292:         constant on valid events, hence orthogonal to the first target-match
293:         and second local-position coefficients as well. A common gate and
294:         norm make information content the main replacement contrast. The
295:         gate can itself carry information; the duplicate isolates that.
296:         """
297:         cubic = self._coarse_residual(
298:             rank * rank * rank, linear, quadratic, valid, total)
299:         scrambled = self._coarse_residual(
300:             scrambled_rank * scrambled_rank * scrambled_rank,
301:             linear, quadratic, valid, total)
302:         cubic_norm2 = cubic.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
303:         scrambled_norm2 = scrambled.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
304:         incumbent_norm2 = incumbent.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
305:         target_norm2 = position.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
306:         occupied = (counts > 0).sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)
307:         support = ((occupied >= 4) & (cubic_norm2 > 1e-10)
308:                    & (scrambled_norm2 > 1e-10)
309:                    & (incumbent_norm2 > 1e-10)
310:                    & (target_norm2 > 1e-10)).to(valid.dtype)
311:         cubic = (cubic * (target_norm2 / cubic_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10)).sqrt()
312:                  * support)
313:         scrambled = (scrambled
314:                      * (target_norm2 / scrambled_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10)).sqrt()
315:                      * support)
316:         duplicate = incumbent * support
317:         # All alternatives above execute in all cells; no modules or RNG added.
318:         if self.coarse_extension == 'cubic':
319:             return cubic
320:         if self.coarse_extension == 'scrambled':
321:             return scrambled
322:         if self.coarse_extension == 'duplicate':
323:             return duplicate
324:         return incumbent
325: 
326:     @staticmethod
327:     def _coarse_residual(raw, linear, quadratic, valid, total):
328:         """Two projection sweeps in FP32; zero bases are harmless."""
329:         residual = valid * raw
330:         linear_norm2 = linear.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
331:         quadratic_norm2 = quadratic.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
332:         for _ in range(2):
333:             mean = residual.sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True) / total.unsqueeze(-1)
334:             residual = valid * (residual - mean)
335:             slope = ((residual * linear).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
336:                      / linear_norm2.clamp_min(1e-12))
337:             residual = valid * (residual - slope * linear)
338:             slope = ((residual * quadratic).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
339:                      / quadratic_norm2.clamp_min(1e-12))
340:             residual = valid * (residual - slope * quadratic)
341:         mean = residual.sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True) / total.unsqueeze(-1)
342:         return valid * (residual - mean)
343: 
344:     def _joint_coefficients(self, affinity, position, fourth, valid, counts,
345:                             rank, scrambled_rank):
346:         """Specialize the inherited available/norm branch without changing it.
347: 
348:         The constructor already requires match_support='available' and
349:         match_scaling='norm'. The discarded projections affect neither this
350:         returned coefficient nor state, RNG, learned values or gradients.
351:         Keep the live expression and operation order unchanged. The caller's
352:         coarse-extension gate (including both residual norms) is retained.
353:         """
354:         position_norm2 = position.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
355:         match_norm2 = affinity.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
356:         available = ((position_norm2 > 1e-10)
357:                      & (match_norm2 > 1e-10)).to(valid.dtype)
358:         available_norm = affinity * (position_norm2 / match_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10)).sqrt() * available
359:         return available_norm
360: 
361:     @staticmethod
362:     def _joint_residual(raw, position, position_norm2, basis, basis_norm2, valid, counts):
363:         residual = valid * (raw - (raw * valid).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
364:                             / counts.clamp_min(1))
365:         for _ in range(2):
366:             slope = ((residual * position).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
367:                      / position_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10))
368:             residual = valid * (residual - slope * position)
369:             slope = ((residual * basis).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
370:                      / basis_norm2.clamp_min(1e-10))
371:             residual = valid * (residual - slope * basis)
372:             residual = valid * (residual - residual.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
373:                                 / counts.clamp_min(1))
374:         return residual
375: 
376:     @staticmethod
377:     def _orthogonal_block_residual(raw, linear, linear_norm2, valid, total):
378:         mean = (raw * valid).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True) / total.unsqueeze(-1)
379:         residual = valid * (raw - mean)
380:         slope = ((residual * linear).sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
381:                  / linear_norm2.clamp_min(1e-12))
382:         residual = valid * (residual - slope * linear)
383:         # Recenter once more to reduce finite-precision constant leakage.
384:         residual_mean = residual.sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True) / total.unsqueeze(-1)
385:         residual = valid * (residual - residual_mean)
386:         return residual, residual.square().sum(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True)
387: 
388:     def _compress_both(self, values, mask, auxiliary):
389:         batch, length, width = values.shape
390:         if length != 100:
391:             raise ValueError('Frozen protocol requires 100 history positions')
392:         groups, block_size = 10, 10
393:         valid = mask.bool().reshape(batch, groups, block_size)
394:         membership = auxiliary.reshape(batch, groups, block_size) & valid
395:         # Per temporal block: one uniform slot and two feedback strata.
396:         # Each branch independently covers every valid event exactly once.
397:         assignment = torch.stack((valid, valid & ~membership, membership), dim=-2)
398:         assignment = assignment.to(values.dtype).reshape(batch * groups, 3, block_size)
399:         counts = assignment.sum(-1)
400:         grouped = values.reshape(batch * groups, block_size, width)
401:         sums = torch.bmm(assignment, grouped)
402:         means = sums / counts.clamp_min(1).unsqueeze(-1)
403:         return means.reshape(batch, groups * 3, width), counts.reshape(batch, groups * 3)
404: 
405:     def _compress_with_match(self, values, mask, auxiliary, match_union):
406:         """Seven rows with population-matched counts and support emptiness.
407: 
408:         Valid-rank rotation operates inside a block, including noncontiguous
409:         validity masks, and preserves target-match cardinality. Special IDs
410:         have already been excluded by _target_match_summary. No labels,
411:         external identities, timestamps, state or RNG enter this assignment.
412:         """
413:         batch, length, width = values.shape
414:         if length != 100:
415:             raise ValueError('Frozen protocol requires 100 history positions')
416:         valid = mask.bool().reshape(batch, 10, 10)
417:         feedback = auxiliary.bool().reshape(batch, 10, 10) & valid
418:         matched = match_union.bool().reshape(batch, 10, 10) & valid
419:         rotated = self._rotate_valid_membership(matched, valid)
420:         # Both support pairs have identical per-block cardinalities and
421:         # empty-slot patterns. Duplicate control removes only aligned value
422:         # grouping; the target-match counts and rotated pair remain present.
423:         first_support = (matched if self.normalization_support == 'aligned_rotated'
424:                          else rotated)
425:         assignment = torch.stack(
426:             (valid, valid & ~feedback, feedback,
427:              valid & ~first_support, first_support,
428:              valid & ~rotated, rotated), dim=-2)
429:         assignment = assignment.to(values.dtype).reshape(batch * 10, 7, 10)
430:         counts = assignment.sum(dim=-1)
431:         sums = torch.bmm(assignment, values.reshape(batch * 10, 10, width))
432:         means = sums / counts.clamp_min(1).unsqueeze(-1)
433:         return means.reshape(batch, 70, width), counts.reshape(batch, 70)
434: 
435:     @staticmethod
436:     def _rotate_valid_membership(matched, valid):
437:         # Pack membership by valid-event rank, rotate by half the valid
438:         # count, then unpack to the original valid positions. Invalid
439:         # entries contribute zero even when scatter indices coincide.
440:         matched = matched & valid
441:         ranks = (valid.long().cumsum(dim=-1) - 1).clamp_min(0)
442:         counts = valid.long().sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
443:         packed = torch.zeros_like(ranks).scatter_add(-1, ranks, matched.long())
444:         source = (ranks + counts // 2).remainder(counts.clamp_min(1))
445:         return packed.gather(-1, source).bool() & valid
446: 
447:     def _pool_seven(self, weights, values, counts):
448:         batch = values.shape[0]
449:         weights = weights.reshape(batch, 70) * counts.to(weights.dtype)
450:         weighted = (weights.unsqueeze(-1) * values).reshape(
451:             batch, 10, 7, self.value_width)
452:         return weighted.sum(dim=1)
453: 
454:     def _interactions(self, target, values):
455:         keys = values[:, :, :self.key_width]
456:         action = values[:, :, self.key_width:]
457:         batch, slots, _ = keys.shape
458:         query = target[:, None, :].expand(-1, slots, -1)
459:         return torch.cat([query, keys, query - keys, query * keys, action], dim=-1).reshape(batch * slots, -1)
460: 
461:     def _primary_activation(self, interactions):
462:         """Forward-identical stop-gradient on nonreadout support rows.
463: 
464:         Flattened order is batch, block, seven strata. The first three strata
465:         retain the incumbent gradient paths. Before EACH Dice, rows 3..6
466:         become constants for moment estimation in the blocked cell. This
467:         removes their backward contribution to the preceding affine layer
468:         and embedding sources, while preserving their forward activations,
469:         batch moments and running-buffer updates at a fixed parameter state.
470:         Selected rows still differentiate through their own batch moments;
471:         shared scorer parameters and later updates can consequently differ.
472:         No extra scorer pass, parameters, persistent state or RNG is added.
473:         """
474:         if not self.training or self.support_gradient == 'attached':
475:             return self.local_activation(interactions)
476:         retained = (torch.arange(interactions.shape[0], device=interactions.device)
477:                     .remainder(7) < 3).unsqueeze(-1)
478:         hidden = interactions
479:         for layer in self.local_activation:
480:             if isinstance(layer, Dice):
481:                 hidden = torch.where(retained, hidden, hidden.detach())
482:             hidden = layer(hidden)
483:         return hidden
484: 
485:     def _auxiliary_activation(self, interactions):
486:         # Functional evaluation uses the SAME learned scorer with parameter
487:         # stop-gradient fixed on. Do not use no_grad: gradients into each
488:         # allowed embedding source must survive the shared scoring operator.
489:         parameters = {
490:             name: (parameter.detach() if self.block_aux_scorer_grad else parameter)
491:             for name, parameter in self.local_activation.named_parameters()
492:         }
493:         # Dice contains BatchNorm running state. Only the primary call may
494:         # update persistent buffers. Cloned auxiliary buffers also prevent an
495:         # in-place second update of state referenced by the first graph.
496:         buffers = {name: buffer.detach().clone()
497:                    for name, buffer in self.local_activation.named_buffers()}
498:         return torch.func.functional_call(
499:             self.local_activation, (parameters, buffers), (interactions,), strict=True)
500: 
501:     def _pool(self, weights, values, counts):
502:         batch, slots, _ = values.shape
503:         weights = weights.reshape(batch, slots) * counts.to(weights.dtype)
504:         weighted = (weights.unsqueeze(-1) * values).reshape(batch, 10, 3, self.value_width)
505:         return weighted.sum(dim=1)
506: 
507:     def forward(self, inputs):
508:         context, target, values, mask, auxiliary, detail, position_detail, block_detail, curvature_detail, joint_detail, match_counts, match_union = self._represent(inputs)
509:         batch = values.shape[0]
510:         all_values, all_counts = self._compress_with_match(values, mask, auxiliary, match_union)
511:         # All four cells score 70 slots; only uniform slots enter the primary

[stat.ML] 13 Sep 2018\n45: Deep Interest Network for Click-Through Rate Prediction\n46: Conference: KDD’18; ; August 19–23, 2018, London, United Kingdom.CCS: Information systems Display advertisingCCS: Information systems Recommender systems\n47: Guorui Zhou, Chengru Song, Xiaoqiang Zhu\n48: Ying Fan, Han Zhu, Xiao Ma, Yanghui Yan, Junqi Jin, Han Li, Kun Gai\n49: Affiliation: Alibaba Group\n50: email: guorui.xgr, chengru.scr, xiaoqiang.zxq, zhuhan.zh, fanying.fy, maxiao.ma, yanghui.yyh, junqi.jjq, lihan.hl,jingshi.gk@alibaba-inc.com\n51: © acmcopyright\n52: Abstract.\n53: Click-through rate prediction is an essential task in industrial applications, such as online advertising.\n54: Recently deep learning based models have been proposed, which follow a similar Embedding&MLP paradigm.\n55: In these methods large scale sparse input features are first mapped into low dimensional embedding vectors, and then transformed into fixed-length vectors in a group-wise manner, finally concatenated together to fed into a multilayer perceptron (MLP) to learn the nonlinear relations among features.\n56: In this way, user features are compressed into a fixed-length representation vector, in regardless of what candidate ads are.\n57: The use of fixed-length vector will be a bottleneck, which brings difficulty for Embedding&MLP methods to capture user’s diverse interests effectively from rich historical behaviors.\n58: In this paper, we propose a novel model: Deep Interest Network (DIN) which tackles this challenge by designing a local activation unit to adaptively learn the representation of user interests from historical behaviors with respect to a certain ad.\n59: This representation vector varies over different ads, improving the expressive ability of model greatly.\n60: Besides, we develop two techniques: mini-batch aware regularization and data adaptive activation function which can help training industrial deep networks with hundreds of millions of parameters.\n61: Experiments on two public datasets as well as an Alibaba real production dataset with over 2 billion samples demonstrate the effectiveness of proposed approaches, which achieve superior performance compared with state-of-the-art methods.\n62: DIN now has been successfully deployed in the online display advertising system in Alibaba, serving the main traffic.\n63: Keywords: Click-Through Rate Prediction, Display Advertising, E-commerce\n64: 1. Introduction\n65: In cost-per-click (CPC) advertising system, advertisements are ranked by the eCPM (effective cost per mille), which is the product of the bid price and CTR (click-through rate), and CTR needs to be predicted by the system. Hence, the performance of CTR prediction model has a direct impact on the final revenue and plays a key role in the advertising system. Modeling CTR prediction has received much attention from both research and industry community.\n66: Recently, inspired by the success of deep learning in computer vision (Huang\n67: et al., ) and natural language processing (Bahdanau\n68: et al., 2015), deep learning based methods have been proposed for CTR prediction task (Shan\n69: et al., ; Covington\n70: et al., 2016; Zhai\n71: et al., 2016; et al., 2016a).\n72: These methods follow a similar Embedding&MLP paradigm: large scale sparse input features are first mapped into low dimensional embedding vectors, and then transformed into fixed-length vectors in a group-wise manner, finally concatenated together to fed into fully connected layers (also known as multilayer perceptron, MLP) to learn the nonlinear relations among features.\n73: Compared with commonly used logistic regression model (Mcmahan\n74: et al., 2014), these deep learning methods can reduce a lot of feature engineering jobs and enhance the model capability greatly. For simplicity, we name these methods Embedding&MLP in this paper, which now have become popular on CTR prediction task.\n75: However, the user representation vector with a limited dimension in Embedding&MLP methods will be a bottleneck to express user’s diverse interests. Take display advertising in e-commerce site as an example. Users might be interested in different kinds of goods simultaneously when visiting the e-commerce site. That is to say, user interests are diverse. When it comes to CTR prediction task, user interests are usually captured from user behavior data.\n76: Embedding&MLP methods learn the representation of all interests for a certain user by transforming the embedding vectors of user behaviors into a fixed-length vector, which is in an euclidean space where all users’ representation vectors are.\n77: In other words, diverse interests of the user are compressed into a fixed-length vector, which limits the expressive ability of Embedding&MLP methods.\n78: To make the representation capable enough for expressing user’s diverse interests, the dimension of the fixed-length vector needs to be largely expanded.\n79: Unfortunately, it will dramatically enlarge the size of learning parameters and aggravate the risk of overfitting under limited data. Besides, it adds the burden of computation and storage, which may not be tolerated for an industrial online system.\n80: On the other hand, it is not necessary to compress all the diverse interests of a certain user into the same vector when predicting a candidate ad because only part of user’s interests will influence his/her action (to click or not to click). For example, a female swimmer will click a recommended goggle mostly due to the bought of bathing suit rather than the shoes in her last week’s shopping list.\n81: Motivated by this, we propose a novel model: Deep Interest Network (DIN), which adaptively calculates the representation vector of user interests by taking into consideration the relevance of historical behaviors given a candidate ad.\n82: By introducing a local activation unit, DIN pays attentions to the related user interests by soft-searching for relevant parts of historical behaviors and takes a weighted sum pooling to obtain the representation of user interests with respect to the candidate ad.\n83: Behaviors with higher relevance to the candidate ad get higher activated weights and dominate the representation of user interests.\n84: We visualize this phenomenon in the experiment section.\n85: In this way, the representation vector of user interests varies over different ads, which improves the expressive ability of model under limited dimension and enables DIN to better capture user’s diverse interests.\n86: Training industrial deep networks with large scale sparse features is of great challenge.\n87: For example, SGD based optimization methods only update those parameters of sparse features appearing in each mini-batch. However, adding with traditional ℓ2\\ell_{2} regularization, the computation turns to be unacceptable, which needs to calculate L2-norm over the whole parameters (with size scaling up to billions in our situation) for each mini-batch. In this paper, we develop a novel mini-batch aware regularization where only parameters of non-zero features appearing in each mini-batch participate in the calculation of L2-norm, making the computation acceptable. Besides, we design a data adaptive activation function, which generalizes commonly used PReLU(He\n88: et al., 2015) by adaptively adjusting the rectified point w.r.t. distribution of inputs and is shown to be helpful for training industrial networks with sparse features.\n89: The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:\n90: •\n91: We point out the limit of using fixed-length vector to express user’s diverse interests and design a novel deep interest network (DIN) which introduces a local activation unit to adaptively learn the representation of user interests from historical behaviors w.r.t. given ads. DIN can improve the expressive ability of model greatly and better capture the diversity characteristic of user interests.\n92: •\n93: We develop two novel techniques to help training industrial deep networks: i) a mini-batch aware regularizer, which saves heavy computation of regularization on deep networks with huge number of parameters and is helpful for avoiding overfitting, ii) a data adaptive activation function, which generalizes PReLU by considering the distribution of inputs and shows well performance.\n94: •\n95: We conduct extensive experiments on both public and Alibaba datasets. Results verify the effectiveness of proposed DIN and training techniques. Our code11\n96: 1\n97: Experiment code on two public datasets is available on GitHub: https://github.com/zhougr1993/DeepInterestNetwork is publicly available. The proposed approaches have been deployed in the commercial display advertising system in Alibaba, one of world’s largest advertising platform, contributing significant improvement to the business.\n98: In this paper we focus on the CTR prediction modeling in the scenario of display advertising in e-commerce industry.\n99: Methods discussed here can be applied in similar scenarios with rich user behaviors, such as personalized recommendation in e-commerce sites, feeds ranking in social networks etc.\n100: The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We discuss related work in section 2 and introduce the background about characteristic of user behavior data in display advertising system of e-commerce site in section 3. Section 4 and 5 describe in detail the design of DIN model as well as two proposed training techniques. We present experiments in section 6 and conclude in section 7.\n101: 2. Relatedwork\n102: The structure of CTR prediction model has evolved from shallow to deep. At the same time, the number of samples and the dimension of features used in CTR model have become larger and larger. In order to better extract feature relations to improve performance, several works pay attention to the design of model structure.\n103: As a pioneer work, NNLM (Bengio Yoshua\n104: et al., 2003) learns distributed representation for each word,\n105: aiming to avoid curse of dimension in language modeling.\n106: This method, often referred to as embedding,\n107: has inspired many natural language models and CTR prediction models that need to handle large-scale sparse inputs.\n108: LS-PLM (Gai\n109: et al., 2017) and FM (Rendle, 2010) models can be viewed as a class of networks with one hidden layer, which first\n110: employs embedding layer on sparse inputs and then imposes specially designed transformation functions for target fitting, aiming to capture the combination relations among features.\n111: Deep Crossing (Shan\n112: et al., ), Wide&Deep Learning (et al., 2016a) and YouTube Recommendation CTR model (Covington\n113: et al., 2016) extend LS-PLM and FM by replacing the transformation function with complex MLP network, which enhances the model capability greatly. PNN(et al., 2016b) tries to capture high-order feature interactions by involving a product layer after embedding layer. DeepFM(Guo\n114: et al., 2017) imposes a factorization machines as \"wide\" module in Wide&Deep (et al., 2016a) with no need of feature engineering.\n115: Overall, these methods follow a similar model structure with combination of embedding layer (for learning the dense representation of sparse features) and MLP (for learning the combination relations of features automatically).\n116: This kind of CTR prediction model reduces the manual feature engineering jobs greatly. Our base model follows this kind of model structure.\n117: However in applications with rich user behaviors, features are often contained with variable-length list of ids, e.g., searched terms or watched videos in YouTube recommender system (Covington\n118: et al., 2016). These models often transform corresponding list of embedding vectors into a fixed-length vector via sum/average pooling, which causes loss of information.\n119: The proposed DIN tackles it by adaptively learning the representation vector w.r.t. given ad, improving the expressive ability of model.\n120: Attention mechanism originates from Neural Machine Translation (NMT) field (Bahdanau\n121: et al., 2015).\n122: NMT takes a weighted sum of all the annotations to get an expected annotation and focuses only on information relevant to the generation of next target word.\n123: A recent work, DeepIntent (Zhai\n124: et al., 2016) applies attention in the context of search advertising. Similar to NMT, they use RNN(Williams and\n125: Zipser, 1989) to model text, then learn one global hidden vector to help paying attention on the key words in each query. It is shown that the use of attention can help capturing the main intent of query or ad.\n126: DIN designs a local activation unit to soft-search for relevant user behaviors and takes a weighted sum pooling to obtain the adaptive representation of user interests with respect to a given ad. The user representation vector varies over different ads, which is different from DeepIntent in which there is no interaction between ad and user.\n127: We make code publicly available, and further show how to successfully deploy DIN in one of the world’s largest advertising systems with novel developed techniques for training large scale deep networks with hundreds of millions of parameters.\n128: 3. Background\n129: In e-commerce sites, such as Alibaba, advertisements are natural goods. In the rest of this paper, without special declaration, we regard ads as goods. Figure 1 briefly illustrates the running procedure of display advertising system in Alibaba, which consists of two main stages: i) matching stage which generates list of candidate ads relevant to the visiting user via methods like collaborative filtering, ii) ranking stage which predicts CTR for each given ad and then selects top ranked ones.\n130: Everyday, hundreds of millions of users visit the e-commerce site, leaving us with lots of user behavior data which contributes critically in building matching and ranking models.\n131: It is worth mentioning that users with rich historical behaviors contain diverse interests.\n132: For example, a young mother has browsed goods including woolen coat, T-shits, earrings, tote bag, leather handbag and children’s coat recently. These behavior data give us hints about her shopping interests.\n133: When she visits the e-commerce site, system displays a suitable ad to her, for example a new handbag.\n134: Obviously the displayed ad only matches or activates part of interests of this mother.\n135: In summary, interests of user with rich behaviors are diverse and could be locally activated given certain ads. We show later in this paper making use of these characteristics plays important role for building CTR prediction model.\n136: Figure 1. Illustration of running procedure of display advertising system in Alibaba, in which user behavior data plays important roles.\n137: 4. Deep Interest Network\n138: Different from sponsored search, users come into display advertising system without explicitly expressed intentions."

The structure of Deep Interest Network\n251: Among all those features of Table 1, user behavior features are critically important and play key roles in modeling user interests in the scenario of e-commerce applications.\n252: Base model obtains a fixed-length representation vector of user interests by pooling all the embedding vectors over the user behavior feature group, as Eq.(1). This representation vector stays the same for a given user, in regardless of what candidate ads are.\n253: In this way, the user representation vector with a limited dimension will be a bottleneck to express user’s diverse interests.\n254: To make it capable enough, an easy method is to expand the dimension of embedding vector, which unfortunately will increase the size of learning parameters heavily.\n255: It will lead to overfitting under limited training data and add the burden of computation and storage, which may not be tolerated for an industrial online system.\n256: Is there an elegant way to represent user’s diverse interests in one vector under limited dimension?\n257: The local activation characteristic of user interests gives us inspiration to design a novel model named deep interest network(DIN).\n258: Imagine when the young mother mentioned above in section 3 visits the e-commerce site, she finds the displayed new handbag cute and clicks it.\n259: Let’s dissect the driving force of click action.\n260: The displayed ad hits the related interests of this young mother by soft-searching her historical behaviors and finding that she had browsed similar goods of tote bag and leather handbag recently.\n261: In other words, behaviors related to displayed ad greatly contribute to the click action.\n262: DIN simulates this process by paying attention to the representation of locally activated interests w.r.t. given ad.\n263: Instead of expressing all user’s diverse interests with the same vector, DIN adaptively calculate the representation vector of user interests by taking into consideration the relevance of historical behaviors w.r.t. candidate ad.\n264: This representation vector varies over different ads.\n265: The right part of Fig.2 illustrates the architecture of DIN.\n266: Compared with base model, DIN introduces a novel designed local activation unit and maintains the other structures the same. In this way, 𝒗U​(A)\\bm{v}_{U}(A) varies over different ads. a⁡(⋅)a(\\cdot) is a feed-forward network with output as the activation weight, as illustrated in Fig.2. Apart from the two input embedding vectors, a⁡(⋅)a(\\cdot) adds the out product of them to feed into the subsequent network, which is an explicit knowledge to help relevance modeling.\n270: Local activation unit of Eq.(3) shares similar ideas with attention methods which are developed in NMT task(Bahdanau\n271: et al., 2015).\n272: However different from traditional attention method, the constraint of ∑iwi=1\\sum_{i}w_{i}=1 is relaxed in Eq.(3), aiming to reserve the intensity of user interests.\n273: That is, normalization with softmax on the output of a⁡(⋅)a(\\cdot) is abandoned.\n274: Instead, value of ∑iwi\\sum_{i}w_{i} is treated as an approximation of the intensity of activated user interests to some degree.\n275: For example, if one user’s historical behaviors contain 90% clothes and 10% electronics.\n276: Given two candidate ads of T-shirt and phone, T-shirt activates most of the historical behaviors belonging to clothes and may get larger value of 𝒗U\\bm{v}_{U} (higher intensity of interest) than phone.\n277: Traditional attention methods lose the resolution on the numerical scale of 𝒗U\\bm{v}_{U} by normalizing of the output of a⁡(⋅)a(\\cdot).\n278: We have tried LSTM to model user historical behavior data in the sequential manner.\n279: But it shows no improvement.\n280: Different from text which is under the constraint of grammar in NLP task, the sequence of user historical behaviors may contain multiple concurrent interests.\n281: Rapid jumping and sudden ending over these interests causes the sequence data of user behaviors to seem to be noisy.\n282: A possible direction is to design special structures to model such data in a sequence way.\n283: We leave it for future research.\n284: 5. Datasets and Experimental Setup\n342: Amazon Dataset22\n343: 2\n344: http://jmcauley.ucsd.edu/data/amazon/.\n345: Amazon Dataset contains product reviews and metadata from Amazon, which is used as benchmark dataset(He and McAuley, 2016; Mcauley\n346: et al., ; Veit\n347: et al., 2015). We conduct experiments on a subset named Electronics, which contains 192,403 users, 63,001 goods, 801 categories and 1,689,188 samples. User behaviors in this dataset are rich, with more than 5 reviews for each users and goods. Features include goods_id, cate_id, user reviewed goods_id_list and cate_id_list. Let all behaviors of a user be (b1,b2,…,bk,…,bnb_{1},b_{2},\\ldots,b_{k},\\ldots,b_{n}), the task is to predict the (k+1)-th reviewed goods by making use of the first k reviewed goods.\n348: Training dataset is generated with k=1,2,…,n−2k=1,2,\\ldots,n-2 for each user. In the test set, we predict the last one given the first n−1n-1 reviewed goods.\n349: For all models, we use SGD as the optimizer with exponential decay, in which learning rate starts at 1 and decay rate is set to 0.1. The mini-batch size is set to be 3232.\n350: MovieLens Dataset33\n351: 3\n352: https://grouplens.org/datasets/movielens/20m/. MovieLens data(Harper and\n353: Konstan, 2015) contains 138,493 users, 27,278 movies, 21 categories and 20,000,263 samples. To make it suitable for CTR prediction task, we transform it into a binary classification data. Original user rating of the movies is continuous value ranging from 0 to 5. We label the samples with rating of 4 and 5 to be positive and the rest to be negative. We segment the data into training and testing dataset based on userID. Among all 138,493 users, of which 100,000 are randomly selected into training set (about 14,470,000 samples) and the rest 38,493 into the test set (about 5,530,000 samples). The task is to predict whether user will rate a given movie to be above 3(positive label) based on historical behaviors. Features include movie_id, movie_cate_id and user rated movie_id_list, movie_cate_id_list. We use the same optimizer, learning rate and mini-batch size as described on Amazon Dataset.\n354: Alibaba Dataset. We collected traffic logs from the online display advertising system in Alibaba, of which two weeks’ samples are used for training and samples of the following day for testing. The size of training and testing set is about 2 billions and 0.14 billion respectively. For all the deep models, the dimensionality of embedding vector is 12 for the whole 16 groups of features.
